item.title: A Global Rebound for Mangroves
item.summary: After decades of decline, this ecologically significant type of forest is making a comeback.
item.page_text:
After decades of decline, this ecologically significant type of forest is making a comeback.
Scientists began using satellites to map mangrove forests in the 1970s after the launch of the first Landsat satellite. For decades, the story they told about mangroves was dominated by loss and decline. Research published in Science suggests that the tide has turned.
A global rebound began around 2010, the scientists found, led by the expansion of mangrove forests in Asia, Australia, and South America. The researchers analyzed Landsat imagery collected between 1984 and 2023, looking for signs of changes in the extent and density of mangrove canopy.
They tallied losses of nearly 3,000 square kilometers (1,200 square miles) between 1984 and 2010, followed by an unexpected increase of nearly 2,000 square kilometers (770 square miles) of mangroves after 2010. They also found that many of today's mangrove forests have denser, more closed canopies than they did in 2010, a sign of healthier, less degraded forests, particularly in South America.
"Other research groups have mapped and analyzed long-term changes in select regions, but these are the first global mangrove maps that cover such a long period," said Zhen Zhang, an environmental scientist at Tulane University. "About two-thirds of the expansion was due to mangroves colonizing new areas and the other third due to restoration and regrowth in degraded areas," he added.
One of the most notable reversals occurred in Southeast Asia—especially Burma (Myanmar). The country lost mangroves rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s due to the expansion of agriculture, aquaculture, and firewood harvesting in coastal areas, but the trend reversed around 2010, when mangrove area began expanding in many places. The authors attribute the turnaround to increased awareness and restoration efforts after the devastating Indian Ocean tsunami in 2004 , strengthened legal protections for forests, and high rates of sedimentation that opened up new mudflats for colonization.
The pair of Landsat images above shows expansion of mangrove forests in Palaw Township in Burma's Myeik District—an area that has seen both significant regeneration of degraded mangrove forests and the spread of trees into new areas since 2010. In this region, much of the regeneration appears to be occurring in abandoned rice fields (brown) south of the village of Kyauktaung. People on nearby Pyin Bukyi Island, meanwhile, have experimented with conservation projects and tree planting efforts to support mangroves. Despite the gains, deforestation remains a common challenge in Burma, which lost 28.6 percent of its mangrove area between the 1980s and 2010. Since then, the country's mangrove area has grown about 10 percent.
Mangrove trees are relatively small—averaging about 13 meters (43 feet)—but mighty from an ecological perspective, with mangrove ecosystems storing up to four times as much carbon as taller inland tropical forests. The trees play an important role in protecting coastal communities from erosion and storm surges, and their distinctive stilt-like roots provide habitat and vital nursery grounds for fish, shrimp, crabs, and other marine life.
In several areas, such as around the mouth of the Amazon River and in northern Australia, extensive deposition of sediment has created new mudflats that mangroves have successfully colonized, contributing to steady increases in each of these regions since the 1990s. At the northern and southern edges of their range, including the southeastern U.S., warming temperatures and fewer freezes have also allowed mangroves to push into areas that were previously too cold, Zhang explained.
There are some areas, however, where losses have outweighed gains. Substantial mangrove losses in the Niger Delta, for instance, have reduced the total mangrove area in West and Central Africa since 2010. North America and southern Africa, meanwhile, have seen widespread degradation after tropical cyclones devastated broad swaths of mangroves. "The global successes we've seen with mangroves during the past decade should not be seen as grounds for complacency," cautioned Zhang. "This underscores that conservation and slowing deforestation can lead to huge positive impacts when coupled with natural expansion and regeneration."
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Adam Voiland.

item.title: UAE's Ras Al Khaimah, Sharjah reopen several beaches after tanker oil spill
item.summary: A satellite image shows an oil spill off the coast of UAE, November 8, 2026. EUROPEAN UNION/COPERNICUS SENTINEL-2 ... satellite images show ...
item.page_text:
DUBAI, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Authorities in the United Arab Emirates’ Ras Al Khaimah and Sharjah emirates said they had reopened several beaches following closures prompted by an oil spill from a tanker damaged in a suspected attack in the Gulf last month.
Sharjah’s media office said the beaches had reopened after authorities brought pollution caused by the spill under control.
“The relevant authorities confirm that the emirate’s beaches and marine environment are safe, allowing the public to visit and enjoy various marine activities safely,” it said.
The spill, which spread along parts of the UAE’s northern coastline, had prompted authorities to close beaches in Ras Al Khaimah, Sharjah and Umm Al Quwain amid concerns over environmental contamination.
The spill has underscored the environmental risks from attacks on commercial shipping in the Gulf since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began in February.
October saw the highest number of attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters since the conflict began, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
In a separate incident, British maritime security firm Ambrey said on Thursday that a merchant vessel had been struck by an unknown projectile about 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah the previous day.
The strike caused a fire in the vessel’s engine room, but no injuries or pollution were reported at the time, Ambrey said.
Shipping through the strait, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies, remains disrupted as uncertainty persists over efforts to reach a US-Iran agreement to end the war and restore maritime traffic.
The spill has also raised concerns about the potential impact on desalination facilities, a crucial source of drinking water in the Gulf, although no shutdowns have been reported.
(Reporting by Jana Choukeir; Editing by Christopher Cushing and Louise Heavens)
DUBAI, 12 novembre (Reuters) - Le autorità degli emirati di Ras Al Khaimah e Sharjah, negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, hanno dichiarato di aver riaperto diverse spiagge dopo le chiusure causate da una fuoriuscita di petrolio da una petroliera danneggiata in un presunto attacco avvenuto nel Golfo il mese scorso.
L’ufficio stampa di Sharjah ha dichiarato che le spiagge sono state riaperte dopo che le autorità hanno riportato sotto controllo l’inquinamento causato dalla fuoriuscita.
“Le autorità competenti confermano che le spiagge e l’ambiente marino dell’emirato sono sicuri, consentendo al pubblico di visitarle e di praticare varie attività marine in tutta sicurezza”, ha affermato.
La fuoriuscita, che si è estesa lungo alcuni tratti della costa settentrionale degli Emirati Arabi Uniti, aveva indotto le autorità a chiudere le spiagge di Ras Al Khaimah, Sharjah e Umm Al Quwain a causa dei timori di contaminazione ambientale.
La fuoriuscita ha messo in evidenza i rischi ambientali derivanti dagli attacchi alla navigazione commerciale nel Golfo da quando, a febbraio, è iniziata la guerra di Stati Uniti e Israele contro l’Iran.
Secondo i dati raccolti dal Washington Institute for Near East Policy, il mese di ottobre ha registrato il numero più elevato di attacchi contro navi mercantili nello Stretto di Hormuz e nelle acque circostanti dall’inizio del conflitto.
In un altro episodio, la società britannica di sicurezza marittima Ambrey ha dichiarato giovedì che il giorno precedente una nave mercantile era stata colpita da un proiettile non identificato a circa 14 miglia nautiche a nord-ovest di Ras Al Khaimah.
L’impatto ha provocato un incendio nella sala macchine della nave, ma al momento non sono stati segnalati feriti né casi di inquinamento, ha precisato Ambrey.
Il traffico marittimo attraverso lo stretto, una rotta vitale per le forniture globali di petrolio e gas, rimane interrotto poiché persiste l’incertezza sugli sforzi per raggiungere un accordo tra Stati Uniti e Iran volto a porre fine alla guerra e ripristinare il traffico marittimo.
La fuoriuscita ha inoltre sollevato preoccupazioni riguardo al potenziale impatto sugli impianti di desalinizzazione, una fonte cruciale di acqua potabile nel Golfo, sebbene non siano state segnalate interruzioni dell’attività.
(Reporter Jana Choukeir; editor Christopher Cushing e Louise Heavens)

item.page_text:
See what super-resolved, cloud-mitigated S2DR outputs look like compared with the original Sentinel-2 imagery, and how they capture change in before/after comparisons. Open the interactive viewer, or download the full 10-band, 16-bit GeoTIFF for deeper analysis.
21 datasets · catalogue updated 12 November 2026
The original 10 m Sentinel-2 image beside the same scene super-resolved to 1 m by S2DR3. The viewer switches between true colour, NDVI and infra-red pseudo-colour.
Sentinel-2 beside S2DR4, which adds cloud, haze and shadow removal to the S2DR3 reconstruction. These open in the earlier S2DR4 viewer, in true colour only, and have no GeoTIFF download.
Two S2DR3 acquisitions of the same area at 1 m, one before an event and one after it. Drag the slider to see what changed.
Each GeoTIFF is the full S2DR3 output for one date: 10 bands (B02–B08, B8A, B11, B12), 16-bit, 1 m pixels.
Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2018–2026), processed by GammaEarth.
Sign up free: the Base Plan includes 75 credits every month to process your own area of interest through Google Colab or the QGIS plugin.

item.summary: The Gulf war is leaving scars so vast they can be seen from space . Satellite images reveal oil slicks spreading across the Strait of Hormuz and ...
item.page_text:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife
The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish. Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster. The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture. Ecosystem at risk The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life. It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development. Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them. Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis. “Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said. “Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.” Strikes and spills Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed. “Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief. More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November. Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain. Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax. An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick. Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites. Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta, two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves. Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war. Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships. According to a Wall Street Journal report, the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island. The damage ahead In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. item.title: Wildfire burn area labeling for insurance - IKT Spīdolas
item.summary: Wildfire burn area labels from Sentinel-2 and Landsat : the fire footprint and the buildings and settlements it reached, for wildfire risk and ...
item.page_text:
Burned land is clear in the shortwave infrared bands of Sentinel-2 and Landsat, even through smoke. We trace the fire perimeter and the unburned islands inside it, then add the exposure layer that matters to an insurer: built-up areas and buildings at the edge or inside the burn. The example is the 2013 Balmoral fire south-west of Sydney.
Footprints are labeled on post-fire imagery compared to a pre-fire scene, so cleared land and shadows are not mistaken for burn. Burn severity classes are available when the model needs more than burned / unburned.
Identify which policies sit inside or next to a burn before inspection.
Historic footprints at the edge of towns, where losses happen, to train and test risk scores.
Past fire activity around a location as an input to pricing.
Sum insured inside a footprint within days of a fire.
Four steps, each ending in something you can check before the next one starts. The satellite image annotation covers formats, quality checks and cost in more detail.
Area, dates and class list agreed in writing, with example images for every class and its edge cases.
Your satellite or drone imagery, or satellite scenes sourced for you: free Sentinel and Landsat, or commercial high-resolution.
You get Scene list with dates and resolution
Annotators work to the guideline. Anything the imagery cannot settle is flagged, not guessed.
You get Labels plus a log of flagged cases
Every class is reviewed against a sample before the data leaves us.
You get Data and per-class accuracy, in your format and CRS
The same fire, a different question. Burn areas for insurance focus on the footprint against buildings; burn scars for forestry focus on the forest that burned and how it recovers.
As soon as there is a clear post-fire image. Sentinel-2 revisits every few days.
That needs high-resolution imagery. See building damage labeling.
